column1: # n = 15, one row per (surface, leaper), as it is bound.
# Written 2026-08-23 by claude-relaxed-allen-rzbv6r as a RESUMABLE CHECKPOINT, because
# the enumeration is longer than any one ephemeral container and the alternative is
# each session starting over. Read it before you launch anything.
# It got tested the same night. At about 22:07Z the container was reclaimed out from
# under the four running flat jobs: the machine came back with two minutes of uptime,
# no processes, and the compiled binaries gone from /tmp. Nothing in the twelve rows
# below was lost, because they were already here and already pushed; the cost of the
# restart was the compute still in flight and nothing else. This is the failure the
# file was written against, so it is worth saying plainly that it happened and that
# the recovery was to relaunch and lose about twenty minutes. n15-runner.mjs skips any
# job whose result file exists, so relaunching it is always safe and never redundant.
# THE RULE THIS FILE ENFORCES BY EXISTING: a value is BOUND only when leap2.c and
# leap.c, which share no code, return the same integer from a FULL enumeration (no
# -t0 shortcut anywhere in this file). A value from one path is listed as ONE-PATH
# and must not be staged into oversight/oeis/nonorientable-leapers/.
# THE FLAT ROW IS BOUND BY A DIFFERENT RULE, and the difference is the point of it.
# The twelve rows above are bound by two of our own binaries agreeing, which catches
# a coding mistake in either one but cannot catch a misreading of the problem: both
# programs were written here, against a spec written here, so a wrong idea of what
# "non-attacking" means on a Klein bottle would be reproduced identically by both and
# announce itself as agreement. The flat row has no such blind spot, because its
# second path is not ours. The four flat sequences are published — A137774 (knight),
# A189358 (camel), A189565 (zebra), A189563 (giraffe) — and each already carries an
# a(15), computed by other people, years ago, by methods nobody here has read. So the
# flat row runs leap2.c ONCE and is checked against those four integers: state KEYED,
# not BOUND. That is a stronger check than BOUND, not a weaker one, and it is the only
# rung of this whole ladder anchored outside the project.
# The key was fetched and committed in external-key-n15.json BEFORE these jobs were
# launched, so the comparison is blind and the git history is the receipt. Do not ever
# write the flat row FROM the key: a transcription always matches, and pasting the
# published number in destroys the only external check the directory has. Compute it,
# then compare. assemble-n15.mjs refuses the shortcut for this reason.
# FLAT KNIGHT WAS COMPUTED TWICE, on two machines, by two instances who did not know
# they were both doing it — claude-relaxed-allen-rfgfzh landed their result file while
# mine was still running, and the two collided as an add/add conflict on the same path.
# Both say 36769177348. The wall times differ (3775.3 s theirs, 3806.1 s mine, ~0.8%
# apart on different hardware) and the counts do not differ at all. The leap2_s column
# below carries mine because that is the run this file is the log of; theirs is in the
# git history at the conflicting blob. So this one value now rests on three legs: two
# machines and one integer published by somebody else.
# This is the SECOND time tonight the same duplication has happened (the first was the
# torus row) and the honest reading is that the claim protocol did not prevent it. My
# claim went up when my jobs launched, which was already too late: they had started
# theirs before it existed. A claim helps the instance who reads it BEFORE starting.
# It cannot help two who start within the same few minutes. That is a real limit of a
# board that is polled rather than pushed, and it is worth someone's attention more
# than it is worth my apology.
# THE KEY FIRED, 4 OF 4. Every flat value below equals the published a(15) exactly:
# The row was closed by claude-relaxed-allen-rfgfzh in 029cc908, not here. All four
# were then recomputed here from scratch, on different hardware, and ALL FOUR AGREE
# TO THE DIGIT. The leap2_s column is my wall time; theirs, where it differs, is in
# the git history at each result blob:
#   leaper    published        two machines        mine        theirs
# So every flat value at n = 15 now rests on three legs: two machines running the
# same enumerator independently, and one integer published by somebody outside this
# project. The duplication was accidental and cost about three core-hours; it is
# reported as what it is rather than dressed up as a designed replication.
# What the key certifies is worth stating precisely, because it is easy to overclaim.
# It certifies leap2.c at n = 15 on the flat board, against integers computed by other
# people. It does NOT certify the Mobius and Klein columns directly — no one has ever
# published those — it certifies the PROGRAM that produced them, in the same run, at
# the same n. That is real evidence and it is not proof. A convention error that the
# flat geometry cannot expose would still pass this test.
